title: Trust Only Each Other

beats.text: The world's most famous stock exchange was born from a crash.
New York, seventeen ninety-two. Everyone wants to lend to William Duer.
He was Hamilton's assistant at the Treasury.
With rich partner Alexander Macomb, he borrows big to corner government bonds.
Short of cash? They sign each other's notes.
Then, in March, Duer stops paying.
Prices fall over twenty percent in weeks. Duer lands in debtors' prison.
So how did that build Wall Street?
You see, borrowing is standing on a friend's shoulders to reach the top shelf.
When he wobbles, you both hit the floor.
Two months later, you and twenty-three brokers sign a deal.
Legend says, under a buttonwood tree.
A minimum fee, and you trade with each other first.
That deal grew into the New York Stock Exchange. Duer never left prison.
He'd borrowed from everybody. So the brokers agreed to trust only each other.

facts.claim: William Duer had been Assistant Secretary of the Treasury under Alexander Hamilton (from 1789), a former Treasury official and Hamilton's friend

Many were eager to lend Duer money; with his wealthy partner Alexander Macomb he borrowed heavily in an attempt to corner/gain control of the market in US government debt securities (late 1791 - early 1792)
Duer and Macomb created their own credit by endorsing one another's notes
Duer stopped paying his creditors in March 1792 (March 9); securities prices fell more than 20% within weeks (nearly a quarter in two weeks)
Duer was put in debtors' prison in March 1792 (Macomb followed in April) and never got out; he died there in 1799
On May 17, 1792, two months after the panic, 24 brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement; legend says under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street (the document itself mentions no tree)
Terms: no commission less than one quarter percent, and 'we will give a preference to each other in our negotiations'
The agreement is regarded as the origin of what became the New York Stock Exchange (New York Stock & Exchange Board, 1817)

caption:
1792: William Duer, Hamilton's former Treasury assistant, borrowed from everyone to corner government bonds. In March he stopped paying, prices fell over 20%, and he went to debtors' prison.
Two months later 24 brokers signed a short deal: a minimum fee, and trade with each other first. It grew into the New York Stock Exchange.
